subject: microbiology
title: Relapsing Fever, Leptospira interrogans, Weil Disease and MAT

steps.tx: **Relapsing fever** is caused by several Borrelia species adapted to lice or soft ticks. After an incubation of several days, abrupt fever, headache, myalgia and sometimes jaundice or bleeding end by crisis, followed by an afebrile interval and one or more relapses. Each relapse is associated with a new antigenic variant of variable major protein, allowing partial escape from the antibody response generated by the preceding wave.
steps.say: Fever that returns in waves should raise antigenic variation by relapsing fever Borrelia.

vis.alt: Relapsing fever Borrelia spirochaetes in a peripheral blood smear
vis.caption: Relapsing fever Borrelia can be numerous enough to see during fever.

steps.tx: Louse borne disease is caused by **Borrelia recurrentis** and spreads between people via body lice in refugee, homelessness and war settings. Tick borne relapsing fever is caused by species such as B hermsii, B turicatae and B duttonii and follows exposure to Ornithodoros soft ticks in cabins, caves or endemic dwellings. Soft ticks feed briefly at night, so patients often never recall a bite.
steps.say: Body lice imply epidemic recurrentis; unnoticed night feeding soft ticks imply tick-borne relapsing fever.

left.title: Louse borne
points: Crowding and inability to change clothes
Often one prolonged initial episode and fewer relapses

steps.tx: Spirochaetes may be visible on **thick and thin blood smears** during febrile peaks, especially with Giemsa or Wright stain, but disappear during afebrile intervals. PCR is more sensitive and can identify species. Serology is less useful acutely because antibodies evolve with antigenic variants. Timing the specimen to fever is therefore a diagnostic intervention, not merely a convenience.
steps.say: Collect blood for relapsing fever microscopy while the patient is febrile, when spirochaetaemia peaks.

left.title: During fever
points: Peripheral smear may show extracellular spirals
Platelets may fall and liver tests rise
Crisis can worsen transiently after antibiotics

right.title: Between episodes
points: Repeat sampling in relapse improves detection

steps.tx: **Leptospira interrogans** is a thin, tightly coiled spirochaete with hooked ends shed in animal urine and surviving in warm freshwater and wet soil. Human infection enters through abraded skin or mucosa during flooding, farming, swimming or occupational exposure. The biphasic illness begins with fever, conjunctival suffusion, calf pain and headache, then may progress to immune phase organ injury.
steps.say: Floodwater exposure plus conjunctival suffusion and calf tenderness is a classic leptospirosis opening.

steps.tx: **Weil disease** is severe leptospirosis with jaundice, acute kidney injury and haemorrhage, sometimes with pulmonary haemorrhage and myocarditis. Despite jaundice, liver failure is usually less dominant than renal and vascular injury. Early doxycycline helps mild disease; severe disease usually receives intravenous penicillin or ceftriaxone with intensive support. Delayed antibiotics do not replace dialysis, transfusion and respiratory care when organ failure is established.
steps.say: Jaundice with renal failure and haemorrhage after water exposure is Weil disease until excluded.

right.title: Management pillars
points: Careful fluids guided by renal and lung status

steps.tx: The **microscopic agglutination test** is the reference leptospirosis serology method. Patient serum is mixed with live leptospiral serovars, and agglutination is read microscopically. It needs paired specimens and a regional serovar panel, so results are slow and laboratory dependent. PCR is most useful in blood during the first week, while IgM assays support later diagnosis but can persist and cross react.
steps.say: MAT is specific reference serology, but early leptospirosis diagnosis often rests on PCR and clinical timing.
